overview.summary: An array is a contiguous block of memory used to store a collection of items of the same type.

Backtracking is an algorithmic technique for solving problems recursively by trying to build a solution incrementally, one piece at a time, removing those solutions that fail to satisfy the constraints of the problem at any point of time.
Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS) are the two fundamental algorithms for traversing or searching tree and graph data structures.
Binary Search is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that finds a target in a sorted array in O(log N) time by repeatedly halving the search space.
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a tree where every left child is smaller than its parent, and every right child is greater.
Dynamic Programming (DP) is a method for solving complex problems by breaking them down into simpler subproblems, and storing the results of those subproblems to avoid redundant calculations.
The fast-and-slow pointer technique (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare) uses two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles, find midpoints, and solve linked list problems.
Graphs model relationships between objects. Unlike trees, graphs can have cycles, multiple parents, and disjoint sections.
Greedy algorithms build up a solution piece by piece, always choosing the next piece that offers the most immediate benefit.
Hash Maps store data in key-value pairs, providing average O(1) time complexity for lookups, insertions, and deletions.
A Heap is a specialized tree-based data structure that satisfies the heap property: the parent node is always larger (or smaller) than its children.
A Linked List is a linear data structure where elements are not stored in contiguous memory. Instead, each element points to the next one.
Prefix Sum is a technique that pre-calculates the cumulative sum of elements in an array to answer range sum queries in O(1) time.
A Queue is a linear data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle.
Recursion is a method where the solution to a problem depends on solutions to smaller instances of the same problem.
Searching algorithms are used to retrieve information stored within some data structure.
Sliding Window turns repeated contiguous-range work into a single flowing pass across the data.
Sorting algorithms arrange elements in a certain order (usually ascending). Understanding how they work internally is crucial for grasping time complexity limits.
Stacks (LIFO) and Queues (FIFO) are the two fundamental restricted-access data structures. Understanding both and knowing when to use which is key.
A Stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle.
A String is an array of characters. However, depending on the language, strings are often immutable.
Trees are hierarchical data structures modeling relationships rather than flat lists.
A Trie (pronounced 'try') is a specialized tree used to store associative data structures, specifically strings. It excels at fast prefix matching.
Two Pointers uses two moving indices to narrow the search space without nested loops.
Vectors (or Dynamic Arrays) are arrays that automatically resize themselves when they run out of space.
